citations.narrative:
The facility failed to keep six fence structures in good repair in the enclosure housing three Emu. These fence structures
surround trees and have broken boards with sharp points, exposed nails, and wire mesh that is broken exposing sharp
points.
Failure to adequately maintain primary enclosures places birds at significant risk. Structural defects or poor upkeep can
result in entanglement, injuries, or even death of the birds housed within.
Housing facilities for birds must be designed and constructed so that they are structurally sound for the species of bird
housed in them. They must be kept in good repair, protect the birds from injury, and restrict other animals from entering
that may negatively affect the welfare of the birds within. Birds that are flight-restricted or cannot fly and are allowed to
roam free within the housing facility or a portion thereof must have access to safety pens, enclosures, or other areas that
offer the birds protection during overnight periods and at times when their activities are not monitored.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility does not maintain an effective pest control program. Ants were observed in the food receptacle in an
enclosure housing three Ring-tailed Lemurs.
Keeping insects out of animal food dishes is important because they can contaminate the food, make it unsafe or
unappealing, and in some cases bite or sting the animals, causing stress or injury. They can also introduce bacteria or
mold that increases the risk of illness. If insects overrun a dish, an animal may stop eating, which can lead to dehydration
or malnutrition, and ongoing infestations can create chronic stress that affects their overall well-being.
An effective program for control of insects, external parasites affecting nonhuman primates, and birds and mammals that
are pests, must be established and maintained so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals and reduce
contamination by pests in animal areas.

The facility failed to keep six fence structures in good repair in the enclosure housing five domestic cows, two Zebu, and
one pig. These fence structures surround trees and have broken boards with sharp points, exposed nails, and wire mesh
that is broken exposing sharp points.
Failure to adequately maintain primary enclosures places animals at significant risk. Structural defects or poor upkeep can
result in entanglement, injuries, or even death of the animals housed within.
The facility must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved. The indoor
and outdoor housing facilities shall be structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals
from injury and to contain the animals.

The facility, which houses three Reeve’s Muntjacs in outdoor enclosures, continues to lack an adequate perimeter fence.
The western side of the enclosure housing two Muntjacs and the northern side of the enclosure housing one Muntjac
does not contain a perimeter fence.
An inadequate perimeter fence leaves the facility vulnerable, creating opportunities for intruders or wild animals to enter
and potentially compromises the safety and well-being of the animals. A perimeter fence protects animals from contact
with unauthorized people and animals. A perimeter fence also acts as a secondary containment system if an animal
escapes from its primary enclosure.
All outdoor housing facilities (i.e., facilities not entirely indoors) must be enclosed by a perimeter fence that is of sufficient
height to keep animals and unauthorized persons out. The fence must be constructed so that it protects the animals in the
facility by restricting animals and unauthorized persons from going through it or under it and having contact with the
animals in the facility, and so that it can function as a secondary containment system for the animals in the facility. It must
be of sufficient distance (at least 3 feet) from the outside of the primary enclosure to prevent physical contact between
animals inside the enclosure and animals or persons outside the perimeter fence.

The facility has an outdoor shelter housing two Victorian Crowned pigeons and three Fantail pigeons that have exposed
heating fixtures, electrical cords, extension cords, and an electrical splitter without protective covering.
Because birds are highly inquisitive, they may peck or chew on unsecured wiring, putting them at risk of shock, burns, or
other serious injuries. Ensuring all electrical components are protected and providing only appropriate, secure perching
options are essential measures for maintaining avian safety and welfare.
Primary enclosures must be designed and constructed of suitable materials so that they are structurally sound. The
primary enclosures must be kept in good repair. Primary enclosures must be constructed and maintained so that they
protect the birds from injury.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
There is an excessive accumulation of excreta on four heating elements, the electrical cords attached to them, and on the
floor of a shelter housing two Victorian Crowned pigeons and three Fantail pigeons.
Organic waste and contaminated surfaces allow germs, parasites, and infectious agents to accumulate and spread.
Waste buildup on heating elements and electrical cords and electrical components is a severe fire hazard which can
cause injury or death.
Excreta and food waste must be removed from primary enclosures and from under and around primary enclosures as
often as necessary to prevent excessive accumulation of feces and food waste, to prevent soiling of the birds contained in
the primary enclosures, and to reduce disease hazards, insects, pests, and odors. When steam or water is used to clean
primary enclosures, measures must be taken to protect birds from being harmed, wetted involuntarily, or distressed in the
process. Standing water, except for such water in pools or other aquatic areas (e.g., ponds, waterfalls, fountains, and
other water features), must be removed from the primary enclosure.
This is a 1st Re-License Inspection for a Class “C" license. The inspection and exit briefing were conducted with the
applicant.
All items must be in compliance within 2 more inspection(s) or by December 6, 2026 or the applicant will forfeit the license
fee and must wait 6 months to reapply. Please contact your inspector to schedule your next Re-License Inspection.
You may appeal this finding in writing by Octobert 15, 2026.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
Regulated activity can continue under your existing USDA license until it expires on October 19, 2026.
